question: Under Section 234 BNSS (Section 211 CrPC), every charge shall state the offence with which the accused is charged, and if the law which creates the offence gives it any specific name:
options: The offence may be described in the charge by that name only
The entire text of the statute must be copied verbatim
The charge must be written in Latin
The punishment must be specified in days
explanation: Section 234(2) BNSS / S. 211(2) CrPC states: 'If the law which creates the offence gives it any specific name, the offence may be described in the charge by that name only.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; specific statutory name suffices.
optionBreakdown.C: Must be in language of court.

learningObjective: Recall contents of charge under S. 211 CrPC / S. 234 BNSS.

question: Under Section 238 BNSS (Section 215 CrPC), no error in stating either the offence or the particulars, nor omission to state them, shall be regarded at any stage of the case as material, unless:
options: The accused was in fact misled by such error or omission, and it has occasioned a failure of justice
The defence counsel raises an oral objection
The error is more than 3 words long
The charge was framed on a Friday
explanation: Section 238 BNSS / S. 215 CrPC mandates that errors in charge are immaterial unless the accused was misled and a failure of justice was occasioned.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; accused misled AND failure of justice occasioned.
optionBreakdown.B: Oral objection alone does not vitiate.

learningObjective: Master curability of errors in charge.

question: Under Section 239 BNSS (Section 216 CrPC), when may a court alter or add to any charge?
options: At any time before judgment is pronounced
Only before prosecution evidence commences
Only with consent of the accused
Only after the accused confesses
explanation: Section 239(1) BNSS / S. 216(1) CrPC provides that any Court may alter or add to any charge at any time before judgment is pronounced.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; at any time before judgment is pronounced.

learningObjective: Recall timing of alteration of charge.

question: What must the court do immediately upon altering or adding to a charge under Section 239(2) BNSS (Section 216(2) CrPC)?
options: Every such alteration or addition shall be read and explained to the accused
Sentence the accused immediately on the new charge
Dismiss the defense counsel
Order fresh investigation by police
explanation: Section 239(2) BNSS / S. 216(2) CrPC requires that the alteration/addition must be read and explained to the accused to protect his right to a fair defence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; read and explained to the accused.

learningObjective: Recall procedure upon altering charge.

question: Under Section 240 BNSS (Section 217 CrPC), whenever a charge is altered or added to by the Court after the commencement of the trial:
options: The prosecutor and the accused shall be allowed to recall or re-summon, and examine with reference to such alteration/addition, any witness who may have been examined
No witness can be recalled under any circumstance
Only prosecution can call fresh witnesses
The trial must be recommenced de novo before another judge
explanation: Section 240 BNSS / S. 217 CrPC guarantees the statutory right of both parties to recall and examine witnesses regarding the altered/added charge.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; right to recall and examine witnesses on altered charge.
optionBreakdown.C: Both prosecution and accused have this right.

learningObjective: Master right to recall witnesses upon alteration of charge.

question: In Willie (William) Slaney v. State of M.P. (AIR 1956 SC 116), what did the Constitution Bench hold regarding total omission to frame a charge or defective charge?
options: Total omission to frame a charge or defective charge does not vitiate conviction unless actual prejudice or failure of justice has been caused to the accused
Any omission to frame a charge makes the conviction void ab initio automatically
The accused must be acquitted without hearing
Omission can only be cured by the Governor
explanation: Willie Slaney Constitution Bench established that procedural defects or omission to frame charge under S. 535/537 (S. 464 CrPC / S. 509 BNSS) do not vitiate conviction unless prejudice is shown.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Willie Slaney prejudice doctrine governs defective charges.

provision: BNSS S. 509 / CrPC S. 464 / Willie Slaney (1956)
learningObjective: Master Willie Slaney prejudice doctrine on charge defects.

question: Under Section 235 BNSS (Section 212 CrPC), what particulars as to time, place and person must the charge contain?
options: Time and place of alleged offence, and the person (if any) against whom, or the thing (if any) in respect of which, it was committed, as are reasonably sufficient to give the accused notice
The date of birth of the judge
The name of the investigating officer's spouse
The vehicle number of the police van
explanation: Section 235 BNSS / S. 212 CrPC mandates particulars of time, place, victim/property to give the accused clear notice of the precise accusation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; time, place, person/property reasonably sufficient to give notice.

learningObjective: Recall particulars of time, place and person in charge.

question: Under Section 235(2) BNSS (Section 212(2) CrPC), in a charge of Criminal Breach of Trust or Dishonest Misappropriation of money, it shall be sufficient to specify:
options: The gross sum in respect of which the offence is alleged to have been committed, and the dates between which the offence is alleged to have been committed (not exceeding one year)
Every single individual rupee transaction with exact time of day
The bank manager's personal salary
Only the final balance left in the account
explanation: Section 235(2) BNSS / S. 212(2) CrPC allows specifying gross sum and dates within a space of one year without specifying particular items/dates.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; gross sum and dates within one year.

learningObjective: Master gross-sum charge rule in CBT/misappropriation.

question: Under Section 236 BNSS (Section 213 CrPC), when must the charge also state the 'manner' of committing the offence?
options: When the nature of the case is such that the particulars mentioned in Sections 211 and 212 do not give the accused sufficient notice of the matter with which he is charged
In every simple theft case
Only in traffic violations
Never
explanation: Section 236 BNSS / S. 213 CrPC provides that when particulars under S. 211/212 do not give sufficient notice (e.g. cheating, obstructing public servant), manner of committing must be stated.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; when general particulars do not give sufficient notice.
optionBreakdown.B: Theft particulars usually suffice without elaborate manner.

learningObjective: Recall when manner of committing offence must be stated.

question: Under Section 234(7) BNSS (Section 211(7) CrPC), if the accused has been previously convicted of any offence and it is intended to prove such previous conviction for the purpose of affecting punishment:
options: The fact, date and place of the previous conviction shall be stated in the charge; but if omitted, the court may add it at any time before sentence is passed
The accused cannot be charged with the second offence
The previous conviction cannot be mentioned under any circumstances
The previous conviction is tried by a separate jury
explanation: Section 234(7) BNSS / S. 211(7) CrPC requires stating previous conviction in charge for enhanced penalty, but permits addition before sentence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; fact, date, place stated in charge or added before sentence.
optionBreakdown.C: Must be stated for enhanced penalty.

learningObjective: Master previous conviction pleading in charge.

question: What is the basic general rule regarding charges and trials under Section 241 BNSS (Section 218 CrPC)?
options: For every distinct offence of which any person is accused there shall be a separate charge, and every such charge shall be tried separately, except in cases mentioned in Sections 242, 243, 244, 246
All offences committed by a person in his lifetime must be tried together in one trial
A person can only be charged with one offence in total
Police decide which charges are tried together
explanation: Section 241 BNSS (Section 218 CrPC) lays down the cardinal rule: for every distinct offence there shall be a separate charge, and every charge tried separately (unless exceptions apply).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; distinct offence separate charge and separate trial.
optionBreakdown.D: Statute and court decide joinder, not police.

learningObjective: Recall basic rule of separate charge and separate trial.

question: Under Section 242 BNSS (Section 219 CrPC), how many offences of the same kind committed within the space of twelve months may be charged with and tried at one trial?
options: Not exceeding three offences
Not exceeding five offences
Any number of offences
Only two offences
explanation: Section 242(1) BNSS / S. 219(1) CrPC provides: when a person is accused of more offences than one of the same kind committed within 12 months, he may be charged with and tried at one trial for any number not exceeding three.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not exceeding three offences of same kind within 12 months.

learningObjective: Master three-offence rule within 12 months under S. 219 CrPC.

question: Under Section 243(1) BNSS (Section 220(1) CrPC), when may a person be charged with and tried at one trial for any number of offences?
options: If in one series of acts so connected together as to form the same transaction, more offences than one are committed by the same person
Whenever the police file a single FIR
Whenever the offences involve the same police station
Whenever committed on the same day of the week
explanation: Section 243(1) BNSS (Section 220(1) CrPC) allows joint trial of all offences committed in one series of acts so connected as to form the 'same transaction'.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; series of acts forming the same transaction.
optionBreakdown.B: FIR does not govern joinder of charges.
optionBreakdown.C: Police station territory not the test.
optionBreakdown.D: Time alone is not the sole test; same transaction is required.

learningObjective: Master 'same transaction' test under S. 220(1) CrPC.

question: In State of A.P. v. Cheemalapati Ganeswara Rao (AIR 1963 SC 1850), what tests were laid down to determine whether a series of acts form the 'same transaction'?
options: Proximity of time, unity or proximity of place, continuity of action, and community of purpose or design
Whether the accused used the same knife
Whether the witnesses were neighbours
Whether the FIR was handwritten or typed
explanation: Cheemalapati Ganeswara Rao laid down the definitive test for 'same transaction': proximity of time, unity of place, continuity of action, and community of purpose.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; proximity of time/place, continuity of action, community of purpose.

learningObjective: Master Cheemalapati same-transaction tests.

question: Under Section 244 BNSS (Section 221 CrPC), what may the court do if a single act or series of acts is of such a nature that it is doubtful which of several offences the facts will constitute?
options: The accused may be charged with having committed all or any of such offences, or in the alternative; and if charged with one, he may be convicted of the other if proved
The court must dismiss the case for doubt
The case must be sent to the Supreme Court
The police officer must be fined
explanation: Section 244 BNSS (Section 221 CrPC) allows alternative/cumulative charges where facts leave it doubtful which offence was committed, and conviction of proved offence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; alternative/cumulative charges and conviction of proved offence.

learningObjective: Recall alternative charges under S. 221 CrPC / S. 244 BNSS.

question: Under Section 245 BNSS (Section 222 CrPC), when a person is charged with an offence consisting of several particulars, and a combination of some of them is proved constituting a minor offence:
options: He may be convicted of the minor offence, though he was not charged with it
He must be acquitted of both offences
He can only be convicted if a new FIR is registered
A fresh trial must be ordered
explanation: Section 245(1) BNSS / S. 222(1) CrPC allows conviction for a cognate minor offence without a separate charge (e.g. charged with murder, convicted of culpable homicide or hurt).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; conviction of minor proved offence without separate charge.
optionBreakdown.B: Cannot be acquitted of minor offence proved.

learningObjective: Master conviction for minor offence under S. 222 CrPC / S. 245 BNSS.

question: Under Section 246 BNSS (Section 223 CrPC), which of the following persons may be charged and tried together?
options: Persons accused of the same offence committed in the course of the same transaction, or persons accused of an offence and persons accused of abetment/attempt
Any two persons who were arrested on the same day in different parts of the city
Any two persons who have the same surname
All persons currently lodged in a district jail
explanation: Section 246 BNSS / S. 223 CrPC enumerates persons who may be tried jointly (clauses a to g: same offence in same transaction, abettors, principals, theft and receiving stolen property).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; persons accused of same offence in same transaction, abettors/attempts.
optionBreakdown.B: Unrelated offences cannot be tried together.

learningObjective: Recall categories of persons who may be tried jointly.

question: Can a person charged with Murder under Section 302 IPC (S. 103 BNS) be convicted of Attempt to Murder or Grievous Hurt under Section 222 CrPC (S. 245 BNSS)?
options: Yes, because they are cognate minor offences forming part of the major charge
No, because a person can only be convicted of the exact section charged
Only if the complainant agrees in writing
Only in the Supreme Court
explanation: Under S. 222 CrPC / S. 245 BNSS, grievous hurt or attempt to murder is a cognate minor offence carved out of murder, permitting conviction without separate charge.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; cognate minor offence conviction is valid.

learningObjective: Apply minor offence conviction doctrine to murder charge.

question: Under Section 247 BNSS (Section 224 CrPC), when a charge containing more heads than one is framed, and a conviction has been had on one or more of them, what may the complainant or prosecutor do with the remaining charges?
options: May, with the consent of the Court, withdraw the remaining charge or charges, which shall have the effect of an acquittal on such charge(s)
Must continue trial on all charges for 5 years
The remaining charges are transferred to High Court
The accused is convicted on all charges automatically
explanation: Section 247 BNSS (Section 224 CrPC) provides for withdrawal of remaining charges on conviction on one of several charges, operating as an acquittal.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; withdraw remaining charges with court consent, operating as acquittal.

learningObjective: Recall withdrawal of remaining charges on multi-head conviction.

question: What is the effect of misjoinder of charges or misjoinder of persons under Section 464 CrPC / Section 509 BNSS?
options: It does not vitiate the finding, sentence or order unless the court is of opinion that a failure of justice has in fact been occasioned thereby
It automatically invalidates the conviction in every case
The case must be dismissed and cannot be retried
The accused is awarded Rs 10 lakhs compensation
explanation: Under S. 464/465 CrPC (S. 509/510 BNSS), misjoinder of charges is a curable irregularity unless a genuine failure of justice has in fact resulted.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; curable irregularity unless failure of justice has in fact been occasioned.
optionBreakdown.C: Retrial can be ordered if prejudice shown.

learningObjective: Master curability of misjoinder of charges.

question: Under Section 248 BNSS (Section 225 CrPC), in every trial before a Court of Session, the prosecution shall be conducted by:
options: A Public Prosecutor
The investigating officer
The complainant's private counsel exclusively
The judicial clerk
explanation: Section 248 BNSS (Section 225 CrPC) mandates: 'In every trial before a Court of Session, the prosecution shall be conducted by a Public Prosecutor.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; conducted by a Public Prosecutor.
optionBreakdown.B: Police IO cannot conduct Sessions trial.
optionBreakdown.C: Private counsel acts only under PP.

learningObjective: Recall who conducts prosecution in Sessions Court.

question: Under Section 250 BNSS (Section 227 CrPC), when shall the Sessions Judge Discharge the accused?
options: If, upon consideration of the record of the case and documents, and hearing the submissions of the accused and prosecution, the Judge considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused
Whenever the accused pleads not guilty
Whenever the public prosecutor is late to court
Only after examining all defence witnesses
explanation: Section 250 BNSS / S. 227 CrPC provides for discharge if the Judge considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding, recording reasons.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; discharge if no sufficient ground for proceeding, recording reasons.
optionBreakdown.B: Pleading not guilty leads to trial.
optionBreakdown.C: Lateness is not ground for discharge.
optionBreakdown.D: Discharge is at threshold before charge.

learningObjective: Recall grounds for discharge in Sessions trial.

question: In Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal ((1979) 3 SCC 4), what principles were laid down for framing of charge vs discharge under Section 227/228 CrPC?
options: The Judge has the power to sift and weigh evidence for the limited purpose of finding whether a prima facie case exists; where materials disclose grave suspicion, charge must be framed
The Judge must act as a mere post office or mouthpiece of the prosecution
The Judge must determine guilt beyond reasonable doubt at the stage of charge
Discharge can only be granted if the complainant consents
explanation: Prafulla Kumar Samal laid down classic principles: court does not conduct roving inquiry or judge guilt beyond doubt; grave suspicion creates prima facie case for charge.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; sift and weigh for prima facie case; grave suspicion justifies charge.
optionBreakdown.B: Rejected; Judge is not a post office.
optionBreakdown.C: Beyond reasonable doubt is post-trial standard.

learningObjective: Master Prafulla Kumar Samal discharge and charge principles.

question: What statutory time limit does Section 250 BNSS introduce for the accused to file an application for discharge?
options: Within a period of sixty days (60 days) from the date of commitment of the case under Section 232
Within 24 hours of arrest
Within one year
No time limit exists
explanation: Section 250 BNSS introduces a revolutionary 60-day deadline from committal for filing a discharge application, preventing endless delays before charge.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within 60 days from committal under BNSS S. 250.

learningObjective: Master 60-day discharge filing reform in BNSS S. 250.

question: Under Section 251(1) BNSS (Section 228(1) CrPC), what must the Sessions Judge do if he considers that the accused has committed an offence which is NOT exclusively triable by Court of Session?
options: May frame a charge and transfer the case for trial to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or any other JMFC, and direct the accused to appear before that Magistrate
Must acquit the accused
Must dismiss the police charge-sheet
Must refer the case to the High Court
explanation: Section 251(1)(a) BNSS / S. 228(1)(a) CrPC provides that if offence is not exclusively triable by Sessions, Judge may frame charge and transfer case to CJM/JMFC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; frame charge and transfer case to CJM/JMFC.

learningObjective: Recall transfer of case by Sessions Court when not exclusively triable.

question: Under Section 252 BNSS (Section 229 CrPC), if the accused pleads guilty to the charge framed by the Sessions Judge:
options: The Judge shall record the plea and may, in his discretion, convict him thereon
The Judge MUST mandatorily convict him automatically without exercising any discretion
The accused must be sentenced to death immediately
The plea of guilty is void in Sessions cases
explanation: Section 252 BNSS / S. 229 CrPC provides that the Judge 'may, in his discretion, convict him thereon'; conviction is discretionary, not mandatory, especially in capital cases.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; record plea and may, in discretion, convict thereon.
optionBreakdown.B: Conviction on plea of guilty is discretionary, not mandatory.
optionBreakdown.C: Discretion exercised cautiously in serious cases.

learningObjective: Master discretionary conviction on plea of guilty in Sessions trial.

question: Under Section 255 BNSS (Section 232 CrPC), when shall the Sessions Judge record an order of Acquittal without calling upon the accused to enter his defence?
options: If, after taking prosecution evidence, examining accused and hearing prosecution and defence, the Judge considers there is no evidence that accused committed the offence
Whenever the defence counsel requests
Immediately after the opening speech of the prosecutor
Only if the complainant withdraws the complaint
explanation: Section 255 BNSS (Section 232 CrPC) provides for mid-trial acquittal if there is no evidence that accused committed offence, without calling for defence evidence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; acquittal if no evidence after prosecution case.
optionBreakdown.D: Sessions trial cannot be casually withdrawn by complainant.

learningObjective: Recall threshold for mid-trial acquittal under S. 232 CrPC / S. 255 BNSS.

question: What major reform does Section 258 BNSS introduce regarding the timeline for pronouncing judgment in a Sessions Trial?
options: Judgment shall be pronounced within thirty days (30 days) from the date of completion of arguments, extendable up to 45 days for reasons recorded in writing
Within 1 year from arguments
Within 24 hours of filing FIR
No timeline exists
explanation: Section 258 BNSS introduces a strict 30-day timeline (extendable to 45 days) for pronouncing judgment after completion of arguments.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within 30 days (extendable to 45 days) under BNSS S. 258.

learningObjective: Master 30-day judgment delivery timeline in BNSS S. 258.

question: In Santa Singh v. State of Punjab ((1976) 4 SCC 190), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding Section 235(2) CrPC (hearing on sentence)?
options: Bifurcation between conviction and sentencing is mandatory; accused MUST be given a separate hearing on sentence and permitted to produce mitigating materials
Hearing on sentence is an empty formality and can be dispensed with
Sentencing hearing is conducted by the police
Death sentence can be pronounced without hearing the accused on sentence
explanation: Santa Singh established that S. 235(2) CrPC / S. 258(2) BNSS is mandatory: court must hold a distinct hearing on sentence to consider aggravating and mitigating factors.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory separate hearing on sentence to present mitigating materials.
optionBreakdown.B: Rejected; essential component of natural justice.
optionBreakdown.D: Death sentence without hearing on sentence is illegal.

provision: BNSS S. 258(2) / CrPC S. 235(2) / Santa Singh (1976)
learningObjective: Master Santa Singh sentencing hearing doctrine.

question: Under Section 256 BNSS (Section 233 CrPC), when the accused is called upon to enter on his defence, he may apply for issue of process to compel attendance of any witness, and the Judge shall issue process UNLESS:
options: He considers that such application should be refused on the ground that it is made for the purpose of vexation or delay or for defeating the ends of justice
The witness lives in another city
The witness does not speak English
The witness is related to the accused
explanation: Section 256(3) BNSS / S. 233(3) CrPC mandates issuing process for defence witnesses unless the judge records that it is for vexation, delay, or defeating justice.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; issue process unless made for vexation, delay or defeating justice.

learningObjective: Recall defence witness summoning rights under S. 233 CrPC.

question: How is the Trial of Warrant Cases by Magistrates bifurcated under Chapter XIX CrPC (Chapter XIX BNSS)?
options: Cases instituted on a police report (Sections 238-243 CrPC / 261-266 BNSS) AND Cases instituted otherwise than on police report (Sections 244-247 CrPC / 267-270 BNSS)
Cases involving money AND cases involving land
Cases during day AND cases during night
There is no bifurcation; single procedure applies
explanation: Warrant trials before Magistrates have distinct procedures: (A) Cases on police report; (B) Cases instituted otherwise than on police report (private complaints).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; bifurcated into police report cases and private complaint cases.

learningObjective: Recall two procedural tracks of warrant trials before Magistrates.

question: Under Section 261 BNSS (Section 238 CrPC), what is the first duty of the Magistrate when a warrant-case instituted on a police report comes before him?
options: Satisfy himself that he has complied with Section 207 CrPC / S. 230 BNSS (furnishing free copies of police report, FIR, statements under S. 161, confessions under S. 164)
Frame charges immediately without giving copies
Demand bail of Rs 10 lakhs
Examine all prosecution witnesses
explanation: Section 261 BNSS / S. 238 CrPC mandates ensuring compliance with S. 207 CrPC (supplying copies of all police documents free to the accused) before proceeding.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; satisfy compliance with S. 207 (supply of free copies).
optionBreakdown.B: Charge cannot be framed before supplying copies.

learningObjective: Recall duty of Magistrate under S. 238 CrPC to verify supply of copies.

question: Under Section 262 BNSS (Section 239 CrPC), when can the Magistrate discharge the accused in a warrant-case instituted on a police report?
options: If, upon considering the police report and documents, and giving the accused and prosecution an opportunity of being heard, the Magistrate considers the charge against the accused to be groundless
Whenever the accused files an affidavit asserting innocence
Whenever the police report is more than 50 pages long
Only if the victim agrees in writing
explanation: Section 262 BNSS / S. 239 CrPC provides for discharge if the Magistrate considers the charge against the accused to be 'groundless', recording reasons.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; discharge if charge is groundless, recording reasons.
optionBreakdown.D: Victim consent not required for legal discharge.

learningObjective: Recall discharge standard in police report warrant trial.

question: In a warrant-case instituted OTHERWISE than on a police report (private complaint), when is evidence taken under Section 267 BNSS (Section 244 CrPC)?
options: Evidence of prosecution witnesses is taken BEFORE framing of charge; Magistrate hears evidence to determine whether a prima facie case for framing charge is made out
Evidence is taken only after the accused confesses
Evidence is never taken in complaint cases
Evidence is taken by police officers in their station
explanation: In private complaint warrant cases, prosecution must lead evidence under S. 244 CrPC / S. 267 BNSS BEFORE charge can be framed under S. 246 CrPC / S. 269 BNSS.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; prosecution evidence is taken before charge in complaint cases.
optionBreakdown.D: Taken before Magistrate in open court.

learningObjective: Master pre-charge evidence in private complaint warrant trials.

question: Under Section 268 BNSS (Section 245(1) CrPC), when does the Magistrate discharge the accused in a private complaint warrant case?
options: If, upon taking all the evidence referred to in Section 244, the Magistrate considers that no case against the accused has been made out which, if unrebutted, would warrant his conviction
Whenever the complainant fails to bring a lawyer
Whenever the accused smiles in court
Only if the High Court directs
explanation: Section 268 BNSS / S. 245(1) CrPC provides discharge if evidence taken unrebutted would not warrant conviction.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; discharge if unrebutted evidence would not warrant conviction.

learningObjective: Recall discharge standard under S. 245(1) CrPC.

question: Can a Magistrate discharge the accused at ANY PREVIOUS STAGE in a private complaint warrant case under Section 268(2) BNSS (Section 245(2) CrPC)?
options: Yes, nothing in subsection (1) shall prevent the Magistrate from discharging the accused at any previous stage of the case if, for reasons to be recorded, he considers the charge groundless
No, Magistrate must examine all 100 witnesses listed before discharge
Only with written approval of Sessions Judge
Discharge at previous stage is unconstitutional
explanation: Section 268(2) BNSS / S. 245(2) CrPC gives explicit power to discharge the accused at any previous stage if the charge is groundless, without waiting for all evidence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; discharge at any previous stage if charge is groundless.
optionBreakdown.B: Need not examine all witnesses if charge is manifestly groundless.

learningObjective: Master premature discharge power under S. 245(2) CrPC.

question: Under Section 265 BNSS (Section 242(3) CrPC), how does the Magistrate proceed with taking prosecution evidence in a police-instituted warrant trial?
options: On date fixed, Magistrate proceeds to take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution; proviso allows cross-examination of witness to be deferred until other witnesses are examined
Witnesses are examined only via written interrogatories
Accused is barred from cross-examining prosecution witnesses
Prosecution evidence is taken behind closed doors secretly
explanation: Section 265 BNSS / S. 242 CrPC provides for taking prosecution evidence, and allows cross-examination to be deferred until other witnesses have been examined.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; takes evidence, with power to defer cross-examination.

learningObjective: Recall procedure for taking prosecution evidence in warrant case.

question: Under Section 272 BNSS (Section 249 CrPC), when the proceedings have been instituted upon complaint, and on any day fixed for hearing the complainant is absent, what may the Magistrate do?
options: If the offence is non-cognizable or compoundable, the Magistrate may, in his discretion, at any time before charge is framed, discharge the accused
Must sentence the complainant to 3 years imprisonment
Must convict the accused in absentia
The case automatically transfers to the High Court
explanation: Section 272 BNSS (Section 249 CrPC) allows discharge of accused on complainant's absence before charge, provided offence is non-cognizable or compoundable.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; discharge accused before charge if offence is non-cognizable or compoundable.

learningObjective: Recall dismissal on complainant's absence under S. 249 CrPC.

question: Under Section 273 BNSS (Section 250 CrPC), what compensation may a Magistrate order the complainant or informant to pay for accusation without reasonable cause?
options: Such compensation not exceeding the amount of fine he is empowered to impose, to the accused for false/frivolous accusation
A flat sum of Rs 10 lakhs in all cases
The complainant's entire house property
No compensation can ever be ordered against a complainant
explanation: Section 273 BNSS / S. 250 CrPC provides compensation against false/frivolous complainant not exceeding the Magistrate's competent fine limit.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; compensation not exceeding competent fine limit.

learningObjective: Master compensation for frivolous accusation under S. 250 CrPC.

question: If the complainant fails to pay compensation ordered under Section 250 CrPC / Section 273 BNSS, what default punishment may be awarded?
options: Simple imprisonment for a term not exceeding thirty days
Rigorous imprisonment for 3 years
Life imprisonment
Community service for 10 years
explanation: Section 273(3) BNSS / S. 250(3) CrPC prescribes simple imprisonment not exceeding thirty days in default of payment of compensation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; simple imprisonment not exceeding thirty days.

learningObjective: Recall default sentence for non-payment of S. 250 compensation.

question: How is a 'Summons Case' distinguished from a 'Warrant Case' under Section 2 BNSS (Section 2(w) & 2(x) CrPC)?
options: Warrant case means a case relating to an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term exceeding two years; Summons case means a case relating to an offence, and not being a warrant case (punishable up to 2 years)
Warrant cases are tried only by High Court; Summons cases by Magistrates
Summons cases involve weapons; Warrant cases do not
There is no difference in sentence threshold
explanation: Under Section 2(w) and 2(x) CrPC (and BNSS S. 2), the dividing line is 2 years imprisonment: exceeding 2 years is Warrant Case; up to 2 years is Summons Case.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; exceeding 2 years is warrant case; up to 2 years is summons case.

learningObjective: Distinguish Summons Case from Warrant Case by sentencing threshold.

question: Is a formal Charge required to be framed in a Summons Trial under Section 274 BNSS (Section 251 CrPC)?
options: No formal charge is framed; only the particulars of the offence of which he is accused shall be stated to him, and he shall be asked whether he pleads guilty or has any defence
Yes, a formal charge with 10 heads must be framed
Yes, charge must be framed by Sessions Judge
No questions can be asked from the accused
explanation: Section 274 BNSS (Section 251 CrPC) states that in summons cases, no formal charge needs to be framed; substance of accusation is stated orally.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; no formal charge needed; particulars stated orally.
optionBreakdown.B: Formal charge is for warrant/sessions trials.

learningObjective: Recall absence of formal charge in Summons Trial.

question: Under Section 279 BNSS (Section 256 CrPC), if the summons has been issued on complaint, and on the day appointed for appearance the complainant does not appear:
options: The Magistrate shall acquit the accused, unless for some reason he thinks it proper to adjourn the hearing to some other day
The accused must be sentenced to 6 months
The complainant's property is attached
The case is dismissed as a civil suit
explanation: Section 279(1) BNSS / S. 256(1) CrPC mandates that upon non-appearance of complainant in summons case, Magistrate shall ACQUIT the accused (operates as final acquittal).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Magistrate shall acquit the accused.
optionBreakdown.D: It is an acquittal, not civil dismissal.

learningObjective: Master mandatory acquittal on non-appearance of complainant in summons trial.

question: What is the difference between non-appearance of complainant in a Warrant Case (S. 249 CrPC) vs Summons Case (S. 256 CrPC)?
options: In a warrant case, non-appearance results in DISCHARGE (before charge); in a summons case, non-appearance results in ACQUITTAL
Both result in acquittal
Both result in discharge
In summons case, accused is sentenced
explanation: Fundamental distinction: under S. 249 CrPC (warrant case), the order is Discharge (fresh complaint possible); under S. 256 CrPC (summons case), it is Acquittal (bars fresh trial under S. 300).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; warrant case = discharge; summons case = acquittal.

learningObjective: Compare non-appearance effect: Discharge (Warrant) vs Acquittal (Summons).

question: Under Section 280 BNSS (Section 257 CrPC), if a complainant at any time before final order satisfies the Magistrate that there are sufficient grounds for permitting him to withdraw his complaint against the accused:
options: The Magistrate may permit him to withdraw the complaint, and shall thereupon acquit the accused
The accused is discharged only
The complainant must be jailed for wasting court time
The case converts into a sessions trial
explanation: Section 280 BNSS / S. 257 CrPC provides that withdrawal of complaint in a summons case results in an order of ACQUITTAL.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; withdrawal of complaint results in acquittal.
optionBreakdown.B: It is an acquittal, not discharge.
optionBreakdown.D: Does not convert to sessions trial.

learningObjective: Recall withdrawal of complaint in summons case operates as acquittal.

question: Under Section 282 BNSS (Section 259 CrPC), when can a Magistrate convert a Summons Case into a Warrant Case?
options: When in the course of trial of a summons-case relating to an offence punishable with imprisonment exceeding six months, it appears to the Magistrate that in interests of justice the offence should be tried in accordance with warrant-case procedure
In all summons cases automatically
Whenever requested by the complainant orally
Only with High Court permission
explanation: Section 282 BNSS / S. 259 CrPC empowers the Magistrate to convert a summons case punishable with more than 6 months into a warrant case in the interests of justice.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; offence exceeding 6 months, in interests of justice.
optionBreakdown.C: Requires judicial satisfaction and >6 months penalty.

learningObjective: Master conversion of summons case into warrant case under S. 259 CrPC.

question: What is the maximum sentence of imprisonment that can be passed in a Summary Trial under Section 285 BNSS (Section 262(2) CrPC)?
options: No sentence of imprisonment for a term exceeding three months shall be passed in the case of any conviction under this Chapter
Imprisonment up to 1 year
Imprisonment up to 6 months
Imprisonment up to 3 years
explanation: Section 285 BNSS (Section 262(2) CrPC) mandates: 'No sentence of imprisonment for a term exceeding three months shall be passed in the case of any conviction under this Chapter.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; maximum three months imprisonment in summary trial.

learningObjective: Recall 3-month maximum imprisonment in summary trials.

question: What is the enhanced threshold for Summary Trial under Section 283 BNSS (Section 260 CrPC) in property offences?
options: Where the value of stolen/misappropriated property does not exceed Rs 20,000 (increased from Rs 2,000 under CrPC)
Does not exceed Rs 2,000
Does not exceed Rs 50,000
Does not exceed Rs 1 lakh
explanation: Section 283 BNSS increased the monetary limit for summary trial in property offences from Rs 2,000 under CrPC S. 260 to Rs 20,000.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; property value up to Rs 20,000 under BNSS S. 283.
optionBreakdown.B: Rs 2,000 was the old CrPC threshold.

learningObjective: Master enhanced summary trial property threshold (Rs 20,000) under BNSS.

question: What procedure is followed in a Summary Trial under Section 285(1) BNSS (Section 262(1) CrPC)?
options: The procedure specified in this Sanhita for the trial of a summons-case shall be followed, except as otherwise provided
Warrant-case procedure
Sessions trial procedure
Military court procedure
explanation: Section 285(1) BNSS / S. 262(1) CrPC specifies that the procedure for trial of summons-cases shall be followed in summary trials.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; summons-case procedure is followed in summary trials.

learningObjective: Recall procedure followed in summary trials.

question: Can a sentence of imprisonment exceeding three months passed in a summary trial be cured under Section 465 CrPC / S. 510 BNSS?
options: No; awarding imprisonment exceeding three months in a summary trial is an illegal sentence going to the root of jurisdiction and is void
Yes, it is a curable irregularity
Yes, if the Sessions Judge approves it
The sentence automatically reduces to three months
explanation: The 3-month limit under S. 262(2) CrPC is an absolute statutory ceiling; exceeding it is an illegal sentence that vitiates the trial.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; illegal sentence that cannot be cured.
optionBreakdown.C: Sessions Judge cannot validate illegal sentence.
optionBreakdown.D: Must be set aside in appeal/revision.

learningObjective: Analyze jurisdictional nullity of exceeding 3-month summary sentence.

question: Under Chapter XXI-A CrPC (Sections 265A-265L / BNSS Sections 289-300), Plea Bargaining is available for offences:
options: Punishable with imprisonment for a term up to seven years, BUT NOT affecting socio-economic condition of the country, offences against women, or offences against children below 14 years
For all offences including murder and rape
Only for capital offences
Only in civil suits
explanation: Section 289 BNSS / S. 265A CrPC restricts plea bargaining to offences punishable up to 7 years, excluding offences affecting socio-economic conditions, women, and children under 14.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; up to 7 years, excluding socio-economic, women, and children under 14.
optionBreakdown.B: Murder and rape are strictly excluded.

learningObjective: Master statutory scope and exclusions of Plea Bargaining.

question: What new time limit does Section 290(1) BNSS introduce for the accused to file an application for Plea Bargaining?
options: Within a period of thirty days (30 days) from the date of framing of charge
At any time before the final appeal in Supreme Court
Within 24 hours of arrest
Within 1 year from conviction
explanation: Section 290(1) BNSS introduces a strict 30-day timeline from framing of charge to file for plea bargaining, curbing late tactical applications.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; within 30 days from date of framing of charge.

learningObjective: Master 30-day plea bargaining application timeline in BNSS S. 290.

question: Under Section 291 BNSS (Section 265B CrPC), how does the court satisfy itself that the plea bargaining application is voluntary?
options: The court shall examine the accused in camera, wherein the other party in the case shall not be present, to satisfy that application was made voluntarily
By asking the police investigating officer
By torturing the accused
By taking a written note from the public prosecutor
explanation: Section 291(4) BNSS / S. 265B(4) CrPC mandates in camera examination of the accused alone to ensure absence of coercion or inducement.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; in camera examination of accused alone to verify voluntariness.

learningObjective: Recall in-camera voluntariness verification in plea bargaining.

question: Under Section 294 BNSS (Section 265E CrPC), if a mutually satisfactory disposition is reached in plea bargaining and the offence prescribes no minimum sentence:
options: The Court may sentence the accused to one-fourth of the punishment provided or extendable for such offence
The Court must acquit the accused unconditionally
The Court must impose maximum 10 years
The Court can only impose a Rs 10 fine
explanation: Under S. 294(d) BNSS / S. 265E(d) CrPC, where no minimum sentence is provided, the Court may sentence the accused to 1/4th of the punishment provided for the offence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; sentence to one-fourth of the prescribed punishment.
optionBreakdown.B: Plea bargaining results in conviction, not unconditional acquittal.
optionBreakdown.C: Sentencing benefit is the core incentive.

learningObjective: Master one-fourth sentencing benefit in plea bargaining.

question: Under Section 294 BNSS (Section 265E CrPC), if the offence prescribes a mandatory minimum punishment, what sentence may the court award in plea bargaining?
options: Half of such minimum punishment provided by law for the offence
One-fourth of the punishment
The full maximum sentence
Immediate release on probation
explanation: Section 294(c) BNSS / S. 265E(c) CrPC provides that where a minimum punishment is prescribed, the court may award half of such minimum punishment.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; half of the minimum punishment.
optionBreakdown.B: One-fourth applies where no minimum is prescribed.
optionBreakdown.C: Incentive is reduction to half of minimum.

learningObjective: Master half-of-minimum sentencing in plea bargaining.

question: Under Section 296 BNSS (Section 265G CrPC), is an appeal maintainable against a judgment delivered in plea bargaining?
options: No appeal shall lie in any court against such judgment, save that a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 or writ petition under Article 226/227 may lie
Yes, regular first appeal lies to High Court as a matter of right
Appeal lies to the Sessions Judge within 30 days
Appeal lies to the District Magistrate
explanation: Section 296 BNSS / S. 265G CrPC gives finality: no appeal lies against a plea bargaining judgment, except constitutional remedies under Art 136/226/227.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; finality of judgment; no statutory appeal lies.

learningObjective: Master finality and bar on appeal in plea bargaining.

question: Under Section 299 BNSS (Section 265K CrPC), statements or facts stated by an accused in a plea bargaining application:
options: Shall not be used for any other purpose except for the purpose of this Chapter
Can be used as a confession in a separate murder trial
Can be published in newspapers
Can be used by the tax department to levy penalties
explanation: Section 299 BNSS / S. 265K CrPC provides absolute statutory immunity: statements in plea bargaining cannot be used for any other purpose or proceeding.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; cannot be used for any other purpose outside Chapter.
optionBreakdown.D: Cannot be used by other departments.

learningObjective: Master confidentiality and statutory immunity of plea bargaining statements.

question: Which groundbreaking revolutionary procedure is introduced in Section 356 BNSS?
options: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of a proclaimed offender who has absconded and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him
Abolition of all criminal trials
Trial by television jury
Automatic death penalty for absconders
explanation: Section 356 BNSS is one of the most significant procedural innovations: conducting trial in absentia of proclaimed offenders who evade justice.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender.

learningObjective: Master groundbreaking Trial in Absentia under BNSS S. 356.

question: Under Section 356(1) BNSS, when can trial in absentia be commenced against a proclaimed offender?
options: Where the person has absconded to evade trial and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, after expiry of ninety days (90 days) from date of framing charge
Immediately upon filing of FIR
Within 24 hours of proclamation
Only after 20 years have passed
explanation: Section 356(1) BNSS provides that after expiry of 90 days from framing of charge, court may commence trial in absentia.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; after expiry of 90 days from framing of charge.
optionBreakdown.B: Charge must be framed and 90 days elapsed.

learningObjective: Recall 90-day waiting period for trial in absentia under BNSS S. 356.

question: Under Section 356(4) BNSS, who must the Court appoint for the defence of an accused being tried in absentia?
options: An advocate for the defence of such person at the expense of the State
The complainant's lawyer
The investigating officer
The court clerk
explanation: Section 356(4) BNSS ensures fair trial in absentia: the Court shall appoint an advocate for the defence of the absconding accused at State expense.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; State legal aid advocate appointed for defence.
optionBreakdown.D: Clerk has no right of audience.

learningObjective: Master state-appointed defence advocate safeguard in trial in absentia.

question: Under Section 356(7) BNSS, what remedy is available to a proclaimed offender convicted in absentia who subsequently appears or is arrested?
options: May prefer an appeal against the conviction to the higher court within thirty days
Can request execution of the judge
Can tear up the trial record
No remedy or appeal is permitted
explanation: Section 356(7) BNSS explicitly preserves the right of appeal: the convicted person may appeal within thirty days of appearance/production.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; appeal within thirty days to higher court.

learningObjective: Recall appeal rights of person convicted in absentia.

question: Under Section 335 BNSS (Section 299 CrPC), when can depositions of prosecution witnesses be recorded in the absence of an absconding accused?
options: When it is proved that an accused person has absconded and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, court may examine witnesses and their depositions may be given in evidence if witness dies or cannot be found
Whenever the accused is taking lunch
In all traffic trials
Depositions can never be recorded in absence of accused
explanation: Section 335 BNSS (Section 299 CrPC) allows recording evidence in absence of absconder to preserve testimony before witnesses die or disappear.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; preserve testimony of witnesses when accused absconds.
optionBreakdown.D: Section 299 CrPC is an express statutory exception.

learningObjective: Master preservation of evidence under S. 299 CrPC / S. 335 BNSS.

question: Under Section 356(2) BNSS, before commencing trial in absentia, the Court shall publish notice of commencement of trial in:
options: A national or local daily newspaper, and give notice to his relative/friend, and paste notice on conspicuous part of house and police station
Only an unlisted blog
A foreign gazette only
Private radio channel
explanation: Section 356(2) BNSS requires multi-channel public notice: daily newspaper, intimation to relatives, and physical affixation on house and police station.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; newspaper, relatives, house and police station affixation.

learningObjective: Recall public notice prerequisites for trial in absentia.

question: Can a person who has previously been convicted of an offence in which he had been charged with the same offence apply for Plea Bargaining under Section 290 BNSS?
options: No; plea bargaining is barred if the accused has previously been convicted of the same offence (Section 290(2) BNSS / S. 265B(2) CrPC)
Yes, repeat offenders have special preference
Yes, up to 10 convictions
Plea bargaining is exclusively for repeat offenders
explanation: Section 290(2) BNSS / S. 265B(2) CrPC requires an affidavit stating the accused has not previously been convicted of the same offence; repeat offenders are barred.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; repeat offenders of same offence are barred from plea bargaining.

learningObjective: Master bar on repeat offenders in plea bargaining.

question: What did the Law Commission of India (142nd and 154th Reports) recommend that led to the introduction of Plea Bargaining in CrPC?
options: Overburdened trial dockets, prolonged undertrial detentions, and the need for mutually satisfactory restorative justice for victims
Abolishing judicial discretion entirely
Privatizing criminal courts
Adopting French inquisitorial system
explanation: Law Commission Reports 142 and 154 recommended plea bargaining to reduce court arrears, unclog jails, and provide victim compensation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; reducing court congestion and providing restorative justice.

learningObjective: Trace legislative history of plea bargaining.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 300 CrPC (person once convicted or acquitted not to be tried for same offence)?
options: Section 337 BNSS
Section 300 BNSS
Section 356 BNSS
Section 482 BNSS
explanation: Section 337 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 300 CrPC (Autrefois Acquit and Autrefois Convict).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 337 BNSS corresponds to Section 300 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.C: Section 356 BNSS is trial in absentia.

learningObjective: Map Section 300 CrPC to Section 337 BNSS.

question: How is Section 300 CrPC (Section 337 BNSS) wider in scope than Article 20(2) of the Constitution?
options: Article 20(2) embodies only 'Autrefois Convict' (prosecuted and punished); Section 300 CrPC embodies BOTH 'Autrefois Convict' AND 'Autrefois Acquit' (bars retrial after acquittal as well)
Article 20(2) applies only to foreigners
Section 300 CrPC applies only in civil cases
There is no difference between them
explanation: Article 20(2) applies only if the person was prosecuted AND punished (convicted); Section 300 CrPC / S. 337 BNSS is wider because it protects against retrial after acquittal as well.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; S. 300 protects against both prior acquittal and conviction.

learningObjective: Compare Article 20(2) with Section 300 CrPC / S. 337 BNSS.

question: Does a 'Discharge' of an accused operate as an Acquittal for the purpose of Section 300 CrPC (Section 337 BNSS)?
options: No; the Explanation to Section 300 CrPC / S. 337 BNSS expressly states that the dismissal of a complaint or the discharge of the accused is NOT an acquittal for the purpose of this section
Yes, discharge bars any subsequent trial forever
Discharge operates as acquittal if ordered on a Monday
Discharge bars trial unless the President permits
explanation: Explanation to S. 300 CrPC / S. 337 BNSS clarifies: dismissal of complaint or discharge of accused is not an acquittal and does not bar a fresh trial on proper grounds.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; discharge is not an acquittal and does not bar retrial.
optionBreakdown.B: Discharge does not bar second prosecution.

provision: BNSS S. 337 Explanation / CrPC S. 300 Explanation
learningObjective: Master rule: Discharge is not Acquittal under S. 300 CrPC.

question: Under Section 337(2) BNSS (Section 300(2) CrPC), a person acquitted or convicted of any offence may be afterwards tried, with the consent of the State Government, for:
options: Any distinct offence for which a separate charge might have been made against him at the former trial under subsection (1) of Section 220 (Section 243 BNSS)
The identical offence again
No offence can ever be tried again
Only tax evasion
explanation: Section 337(2) BNSS / S. 300(2) CrPC permits second trial for distinct offence within same transaction with State Government consent.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; distinct offence under S. 220(1) with State Government consent.

learningObjective: Master statutory exceptions to double jeopardy under S. 300(2).

question: Under Section 337(3) BNSS (Section 300(3) CrPC), if A is convicted of causing grievous hurt to B, and B subsequently dies of those injuries:
options: A may be afterwards tried for Culpable Homicide or Murder, because the consequences had not happened when he was first tried
A cannot be tried for murder because he was already convicted of hurt
A is automatically sentenced to death without trial
The earlier conviction is converted to murder by court clerk
explanation: Section 337(3) BNSS / S. 300(3) CrPC provides an exception where consequences (death) ensued subsequent to conviction; trial for homicide is competent.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; can be tried for homicide as consequences had not occurred at first trial.
optionBreakdown.B: Prior hurt trial does not bar subsequent homicide trial upon death.

learningObjective: Master subsequent consequence exception to double jeopardy.

question: In Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay (AIR 1953 SC 325), confiscation of gold by Customs authorities under the Sea Customs Act was held:
options: Not to be a prosecution and punishment by a 'court or judicial tribunal'; hence subsequent criminal prosecution under FERA was NOT barred under Article 20(2)
To bar any criminal trial under Article 20(2)
To be unconstitutional
To be an acquittal
explanation: Maqbool Hussain settled that administrative/revenue penalties (customs confiscation) do not constitute judicial prosecution, so double jeopardy does not apply to subsequent penal trial.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; administrative confiscation is not judicial prosecution; penal trial not barred.

learningObjective: Master Maqbool Hussain judicial tribunal test for double jeopardy.

question: Can a departmental disciplinary inquiry against a government servant bar subsequent criminal trial on the same charges?
options: No; departmental proceedings are not a criminal trial before a court of law; both can proceed concurrently and acquittal in one does not automatically bar the other (State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena)
Yes, departmental finding binds the criminal court
Criminal trial is barred if departmental inquiry exonerated him
Departmental inquiry is a judicial trial under Section 300 CrPC
explanation: B.K. Meena ((1996) 6 SCC 417) settled that departmental proceedings and criminal trials serve distinct purposes; departmental inquiry does not bar criminal trial.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; departmental inquiry is not a criminal trial and does not bar prosecution.
optionBreakdown.C: Different standard of proof (preponderance vs reasonable doubt).

learningObjective: Distinguish departmental proceedings from criminal trial under double jeopardy.

question: Under Section 337(6) BNSS (Section 300(6) CrPC), nothing in this section shall affect the provisions of:
options: Section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897
The Income Tax Act
The Transfer of Property Act
The Indian Contract Act
explanation: Section 337(6) BNSS / S. 300(6) CrPC explicitly preserves Section 26 of the General Clauses Act (offence under two enactments: prosecuted under either, but not punished twice).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; preserves Section 26 of General Clauses Act, 1897.

learningObjective: Recall interaction with Section 26 General Clauses Act.

question: What is the doctrine of 'Issue Estoppel' in criminal jurisprudence as recognized in Pritam Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1956 SC 415)?
options: Once a finding of fact has been decided in favor of the accused in a previous trial, that same finding cannot be reopened or litigated against him in a subsequent prosecution
Accused is estopped from proving his innocence
Prosecution can change facts at will
Applies only to civil title disputes
explanation: Pritam Singh and Piara Singh established that issue estoppel bars the prosecution from adducing evidence to controvert a specific finding of fact settled in an earlier trial.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; settled finding of fact in former trial cannot be relitigated against accused.

learningObjective: Master Issue Estoppel in criminal jurisprudence.

question: If a court had no competent jurisdiction to try the offence in the first instance, does an acquittal by that court bar a subsequent trial by a competent court under Section 300 CrPC?
options: No; a trial by a court having no jurisdiction is coram non judice (null and void); hence the acquittal does not bar a subsequent trial by a competent court
Yes, any acquittal by any person bars retrial forever
Yes, jurisdiction is immaterial for double jeopardy
The second trial can only proceed with Supreme Court order
explanation: Mohd. Safi v. State of West Bengal (AIR 1966 SC 69) settled that for S. 300 to apply, the former court must have been a court of competent jurisdiction; a void order bars nothing.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; lack of jurisdiction renders trial void, so S. 300 does not bar retrial.
optionBreakdown.B: Competent jurisdiction is an indispensable prerequisite.

learningObjective: Master requirement of competent jurisdiction for double jeopardy.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 313 CrPC (power to examine the accused)?
options: Section 351 BNSS
Section 313 BNSS
Section 337 BNSS
Section 356 BNSS
explanation: Section 351 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 313 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 351 BNSS corresponds to Section 313 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.D: Section 356 BNSS is trial in absentia.

learningObjective: Map Section 313 CrPC to Section 351 BNSS.

question: Under Section 351(1)(b) BNSS (Section 313(1)(b) CrPC), when is it MANDATORY for the court to question the accused generally on the case?
options: After the witnesses for the prosecution have been examined and before he is called on for his defence
Before prosecution evidence begins
During police interrogation
Only after the judgment is signed
explanation: Section 351(1)(b) BNSS / S. 313(1)(b) CrPC mandates that the Court SHALL question him generally after prosecution witnesses are examined and before defence is called.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory after prosecution evidence and before defence.

learningObjective: Recall mandatory stage of examining accused under S. 313 CrPC.

question: Is an oath administered to the accused when examined under Section 313 CrPC (Section 351 BNSS)?
options: No oath shall be administered to the accused when he is examined under this section (Section 351(2) BNSS / S. 313(2) CrPC)
Yes, oath is mandatory
Administered only if requested by prosecutor
Administered only in murder cases
explanation: Section 351(2) BNSS / S. 313(2) CrPC expressly provides: 'No oath shall be administered to the accused when he is examined under this section.'

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; no oath is administered under S. 313 CrPC / S. 351 BNSS.

learningObjective: Recall prohibition of oath under S. 313 CrPC.

question: What is the consequence if an accused refuses to answer questions or gives false answers under Section 351(3) BNSS (Section 313(3) CrPC)?
options: He shall not render himself liable to punishment by reason only of such refusal, or by giving false answers
He shall be sentenced to 6 months for perjury
He is automatically convicted of the offence
He loses his right to bail
explanation: Section 351(3) BNSS / S. 313(3) CrPC provides that the accused does not commit perjury or punishment by refusing to answer or giving false answers (right against self-incrimination).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; not liable to punishment for refusal or false answers.

learningObjective: Master immunity from perjury under S. 313 CrPC.

question: In Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra ((1984) 4 SCC 116), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding incriminating circumstances NOT put to the accused under S. 313 CrPC?
options: Any incriminating circumstance not put to the accused in his examination under Section 313 CANNOT be used against him and must be completely excluded from consideration
Court can use any evidence even if not put to accused
Prosecutor can put it in written arguments instead
The omission is a curable typographical error
explanation: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda established the bedrock rule: an incriminating circumstance not put to the accused under S. 313 cannot be used to convict him.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; must be excluded from consideration if not put to accused.

learningObjective: Master Sharad Birdhichand Sarda S. 313 exclusion doctrine.

question: Under Section 343 BNSS (Section 306 CrPC), who may Tender a Pardon to an accomplice?
options: Chief Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate at any stage of investigation, inquiry or trial; and Magistrate First Class at any stage of inquiry or trial
The investigating officer at police station
The defence counsel
The victim's family
explanation: Section 343 BNSS (Section 306 CrPC) empowers the CJM/Metropolitan Magistrate (at investigation, inquiry, trial) or JMFC (at inquiry, trial) to tender pardon.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; CJM/JMFC within their respective statutory stages.

learningObjective: Recall authorities empowered to tender pardon to accomplice.

question: On what condition is a Pardon tendered under Section 343(1) BNSS (Section 306(1) CrPC)?
options: On condition of his making a full and true disclosure of the whole of the circumstances within his knowledge relative to the offence and to every other person concerned
On condition of paying Rs 5 lakhs fine
On condition of leaving India immediately
On condition of becoming a police informer
explanation: Section 343(1) BNSS / S. 306(1) CrPC provides that pardon is conditional on making a full and true disclosure of the whole circumstances and accomplices.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; full and true disclosure of whole circumstances and persons concerned.
optionBreakdown.D: Must testify in court as witness.

learningObjective: Recall statutory condition for tender of pardon.

question: Under Section 343(4) BNSS (Section 306(4) CrPC), every person accepting a tender of pardon shall be:
options: Examined as a witness in the court of the Magistrate taking cognizance and in subsequent trial, and shall, unless already on bail, be detained in custody until the termination of trial
Released unconditionally without testifying
Tried jointly with other co-accused
Allowed to retract his statement without penalty
explanation: Section 343(4) BNSS / S. 306(4) CrPC mandates that approver must be examined as a witness and kept in custody (if not on bail) until trial terminates.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; examined as witness and detained in custody until trial ends.
optionBreakdown.C: Cannot be tried jointly once pardoned.
optionBreakdown.D: Retraction leads to trial under S. 308 CrPC.

learningObjective: Master approver custody and examination obligations.

question: Under Section 345 BNSS (Section 308 CrPC), what happens if the Public Prosecutor certifies that the pardoned person has failed to comply with the condition by wilfully concealing anything essential or giving false evidence?
options: Such person may be tried for the offence in respect of which the pardon was tendered, or for any other offence of which he appears to have been guilty in connection with the same matter, and for perjury
The person is hanged immediately without trial
The public prosecutor is removed from service
The co-accused are automatically acquitted
explanation: Section 345 BNSS / S. 308 CrPC provides that upon PP certificate of breach, the approver forfeits pardon and can be tried for the original offence and perjury.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; tried for original offence and perjury upon PP certificate of breach.

learningObjective: Master forfeiture of pardon and trial of approver under S. 308 CrPC.

question: In Suresh Chandra Bahri v. State of Bihar (AIR 1994 SC 2420), what was held regarding the detention of an approver in custody under Section 306(4)(b) CrPC?
options: The object of detaining the approver in custody is to protect him from the wrath of co-accused and ensure he is not influenced or bribed by corrupt means
It is intended as punishment before conviction
It violates Article 21 and is unconstitutional
He can be detained in the police station lockup
explanation: Suresh Chandra Bahri settled that approver custody is protective (to shield him from vengeance and prevent tampering), not punitive.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; protective custody to shield from co-accused and tampering.
optionBreakdown.D: Must be in judicial custody, not police lockup.

learningObjective: Analyze protective rationale of approver detention.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to the famous Section 482 CrPC (saving of inherent powers of High Court)?
options: Section 528 BNSS
Section 482 BNSS
Section 530 BNSS
Section 500 BNSS
explanation: Section 528 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 482 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 528 BNSS corresponds to Section 482 CrPC.

learningObjective: Map Section 482 CrPC to Section 528 BNSS.

question: For what three purposes may the High Court exercise its Inherent Powers under Section 528 BNSS (Section 482 CrPC)?
options: (1) To give effect to any order under this Sanhita; (2) To prevent abuse of the process of any Court; (3) Otherwise to secure the ends of justice
To enact new penal laws
To appoint police officers
To grant bail to all accused without hearing
explanation: Section 528 BNSS / S. 482 CrPC specifies three purposes: give effect to orders, prevent abuse of court process, or secure ends of justice.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; three statutory purposes under Section 482 CrPC / Section 528 BNSS.

learningObjective: Recall three statutory purposes of Section 482 CrPC inherent powers.

question: In State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (AIR 1992 SC 604), how many illustrative categories were formulated by the Supreme Court for quashing an FIR or criminal proceeding under Section 482 CrPC?
options: Seven illustrative categories
Three categories
Ten categories
Five categories
explanation: Bhajan Lal laid down the celebrated seven illustrative categories/guidelines where High Court can exercise S. 482 powers to quash proceedings.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; seven illustrative guidelines in Bhajan Lal.

learningObjective: Master seven Bhajan Lal quashing guidelines under S. 482 CrPC.

question: Which court alone possesses Inherent Powers under Section 528 BNSS (Section 482 CrPC)?
options: The High Court exclusively
The Sessions Court
The Chief Judicial Magistrate
All criminal courts
explanation: Section 528 BNSS / S. 482 CrPC explicitly saves the inherent powers of the 'High Court' only; subordinate courts have no inherent powers.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; High Court exclusively.
optionBreakdown.B: Sessions Court has no inherent powers (Bindeshwari Prasad Singh).
optionBreakdown.D: Subordinate courts are creature of statute.

learningObjective: Master exclusivity of Inherent Powers to High Court.

question: Which provision of BNSS 2023 corresponds to Section 319 CrPC (power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence)?
options: Section 358 BNSS
Section 319 BNSS
Section 351 BNSS
Section 337 BNSS
explanation: Section 358 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 319 CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 358 BNSS corresponds to Section 319 CrPC.

learningObjective: Map Section 319 CrPC to Section 358 BNSS.

question: In the Constitution Bench decision of Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab ((2014) 3 SCC 92), what standard of proof was laid down for summoning an additional accused under Section 319 CrPC?
options: The test is more than prima facie case as at the stage of framing charge, but short of satisfaction beyond reasonable doubt; there must be strong and cogent evidence indicating reasonable prospect of conviction
Mere suspicion or allegation in FIR is sufficient
Proof beyond all reasonable doubt is required
Only if the accused confesses orally
explanation: Hardeep Singh Constitution Bench ruled that S. 319 power is extraordinary, requiring a standard higher than prima facie charge, but not proof beyond reasonable doubt.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; higher than prima facie charge, strong and cogent evidence.

learningObjective: Master Hardeep Singh standard of proof under S. 319 CrPC.

question: Can a person named in the FIR but NOT charge-sheeted by police be summoned under Section 319 CrPC (Section 358 BNSS)?
options: Yes; if evidence adduced during inquiry or trial shows his involvement, he can be summoned even if dropped or not charge-sheeted by police (Hardeep Singh)
No, police charge-sheet is binding on the court
Only if the police agree in writing
Only if the High Court permits
explanation: Hardeep Singh established that person named in FIR but omitted in charge-sheet can be summoned under S. 319 if evidence at trial implicates him.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; can be summoned on evidence adduced at trial.
optionBreakdown.B: Court not bound by police omission.

learningObjective: Recall summoning of non-charge-sheeted persons under S. 319 CrPC.

question: In Gian Singh v. State of Punjab ((2012) 10 SCC 303), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding quashing criminal proceedings on compromise under Section 482 CrPC?
options: High Court under Section 482 can quash criminal proceedings in commercial, financial, matrimonial or civil disputes upon compromise, BUT cannot quash heinous offences like murder, rape, dacoity, or corruption
High Court can quash murder and rape cases upon compromise
Plea bargaining and S. 482 compromise are identical
Compromise can never be accepted in non-compoundable offences
explanation: Gian Singh and Narinder Singh held that High Court can quash non-compoundable private/commercial/matrimonial cases under S. 482 upon settlement, but heinous crimes cannot be quashed.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; quashable in private/matrimonial/commercial disputes, but barred in heinous crimes.
optionBreakdown.D: Section 482 overcomes S. 320 for private disputes.

learningObjective: Master Gian Singh guidelines on quashing upon compromise under S. 482.

question: Can the High Court exercise inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC where there is an express statutory bar in the Code (e.g. against interlocutory revisions under S. 397(2))?
options: Inherent powers cannot be exercised to bypass or defeat an express statutory prohibition in the Code, except in rarest of rare cases where an order is completely without jurisdiction
Yes, Section 482 overrides every written word in all laws
High Court has power to ignore Parliament
Section 482 is superior to the Constitution
explanation: Madhu Limaye and Rajan Kumar Machananda settled that inherent powers cannot be exercised against an express statutory bar like S. 397(2) interlocutory bar.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; inherent power cannot defeat express statutory bar.

learningObjective: Master interplay between S. 482 inherent powers and express statutory bars.

question: What happens to the trial when a new person is summoned as an accused under Section 319 CrPC (Section 358 BNSS)?
options: The proceedings in respect of such person shall be commenced afresh, and the witnesses re-heard in his presence
The new accused is convicted on the evidence already recorded
The earlier trial is cancelled and started from FIR
The new accused cannot cross-examine earlier witnesses
explanation: Section 358(4) BNSS / S. 319(4) CrPC mandates that proceedings against the newly added accused must commence afresh and witnesses re-heard to satisfy natural justice.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; proceedings commence afresh and witnesses re-heard.
optionBreakdown.B: Cannot convict on evidence recorded in his absence.
optionBreakdown.C: Earlier trial not cancelled; newly added person gets de novo evidence.

learningObjective: Master de novo evidence requirement upon adding accused under S. 319 CrPC.

question: How is a 'Bailable Offence' defined under Section 2(b) BNSS (Section 2(a) CrPC)?
options: An offence which is shown as bailable in the First Schedule, or which is made bailable by any other law; and 'non-bailable offence' means any other offence
Any offence where punishment is less than 10 years
An offence where police officer likes the accused
An offence where fine is less than Rs 1,000
explanation: Section 2(b) BNSS / S. 2(a) CrPC defines bailable offence strictly by reference to the First Schedule or specific law; non-bailable is any other offence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; defined by reference to First Schedule or other law.
optionBreakdown.B: Sentence length is descriptive, not statutory definition.

learningObjective: Define Bailable and Non-Bailable offences.

question: Under Section 478 BNSS (Section 436 CrPC), when a person accused of a Bailable Offence is arrested without warrant and is prepared to give bail:
options: Such person SHALL be released on bail as a matter of absolute statutory right
The police or Magistrate has complete discretion to refuse bail
Bail can only be granted by the High Court
He must be detained for at least 7 days
explanation: Section 478 BNSS (Section 436 CrPC) makes bail in bailable offences an absolute, non-discretionary statutory right (Rasiklal v. Kishore Khanchand Wadhwani).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory release on bail as an absolute right.
optionBreakdown.C: Police officer or Magistrate must grant bail.
optionBreakdown.D: Detention when prepared to give bail is illegal.

learningObjective: Master absolute right to bail in bailable offences.

question: Under the Proviso to Section 478(1) BNSS (Section 436(1) CrPC), what must the officer or court do if the person accused of a bailable offence is indigent and unable to furnish surety?
options: Shall discharge him on his executing a bond without sureties (personal bond); and if unable to give bail within a week of arrest, he shall be presumed to be indigent
Send him to jail for 1 year
Demand cash deposit of Rs 10,000
Auction his clothes
explanation: The Proviso to S. 478(1) BNSS / S. 436(1) CrPC mandates release of indigent persons on personal recognizance bond without sureties, presuming indigence if unable to give bail within 1 week.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; release on personal bond without sureties; 1 week indigence presumption.

provision: BNSS S. 478(1) Proviso / CrPC S. 436(1) Proviso
learningObjective: Master indigent release on personal bond under S. 436 CrPC.

question: Under Section 480(1) BNSS (Section 437(1) CrPC), when can a Magistrate NOT release an accused on bail in a non-bailable offence?
options: If there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, subject to specific provisos
Whenever the police oppose bail orally
In all cases where the accused is male
In all offences punishable with more than 1 year
explanation: Section 480(1) BNSS / S. 437(1) CrPC bars Magistrate from granting bail if reasonable grounds exist for believing guilt of offence punishable with death or life imprisonment.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory bar where reasonable grounds for death/life sentence exist.
optionBreakdown.B: Oral police opposition does not bar bail.

learningObjective: Master statutory bar on Magistrate bail in capital/life offences.

question: Under the First Proviso to Section 480(1) BNSS (Section 437(1) CrPC), which persons may be released on bail by a Magistrate EVEN IF the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment?
options: A person under the age of sixteen years, a woman, or a sick or infirm person
Any government servant
Any rich industrialist
Any person having an advocate
explanation: First Proviso to S. 480(1) BNSS / S. 437(1) CrPC creates a benevolent exception: court may grant bail if person is under 16, a woman, or sick/infirm.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; under 16 years, woman, sick or infirm person.

provision: BNSS S. 480(1) Proviso / CrPC S. 437(1) Proviso
learningObjective: Master benevolent bail exception for minors, women, sick/infirm.

question: In State of Rajasthan v. Balchand (AIR 1977 SC 2447), what classic principle was articulated by Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer?
options: 'The basic rule may perhaps be tersely put as bail, not jail, except where there are circumstances suggestive of fleeing from justice or thwarting the course of justice'
'Jail is the rule and bail is an exceptional rarity'
'All undertrials must remain in custody until acquitted'
'Bail should be granted only on payment of heavy cash'
explanation: Balchand established the celebrated maxim of Indian criminal jurisprudence: 'Bail is the rule, jail is the exception'.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; 'Bail, not jail' celebrated doctrine.

learningObjective: Master 'Bail, not jail' principle in Balchand.
