question: Under Section 480(3) BNSS (Section 437(3) CrPC), what conditions may a court impose when releasing an accused on bail for an offence punishable with 7+ years?
options: Attend in accordance with bond conditions, not commit an offence similar to the offence accused of, and not make any inducement/threat/promise to witnesses
Must deposit his salary in the court every month
Must report to police station every 15 minutes
Must surrender his voting rights
explanation: Section 480(3) BNSS / S. 437(3) CrPC specifies statutory bail conditions: attendance, not repeating offence, and not tampering with witnesses/evidence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory conditions regarding attendance, non-repetition, non-tampering.

learningObjective: Recall statutory conditions imposed on bail under S. 437(3) CrPC.

question: What is the difference between Rejection of Bail and Cancellation of Bail under Section 437(5) / 439(2) CrPC?
options: Rejection occurs at the initial stage based on prima facie allegations; Cancellation requires cogent supervening circumstances such as tampering, misuse of liberty, or subversion of justice (Puran v. Rambilas)
Cancellation is automatic whenever complainant appeals
There is no difference between them
Rejection can only be by High Court; cancellation by police
explanation: Puran v. Rambilas ((2001) 6 SCC 338) established that cancellation requires much higher grounds (supervening abuse of liberty/tampering) than initial rejection.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; cancellation requires cogent supervening circumstances/misuse of liberty.

learningObjective: Distinguish rejection of bail from cancellation of bail.

question: Under Section 480(6) BNSS (Section 437(6) CrPC), in a trial of a non-bailable offence before a Magistrate, if trial is not concluded within sixty days from the first date fixed for taking evidence:
options: The accused shall, if in custody during the whole of the said period, be released on bail unless for reasons to be recorded the Magistrate otherwise directs
The accused is automatically acquitted
The trial is transferred to Sessions Court
The witnesses are sent to jail
explanation: Section 480(6) BNSS / S. 437(6) CrPC provides a 60-day trial delay bail: if trial before Magistrate not concluded within 60 days from first evidence date, accused entitled to bail.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; released on bail if trial not concluded within 60 days from first evidence date.

learningObjective: Master 60-day trial delay bail under S. 437(6) CrPC.

question: Under Section 480(7) BNSS (Section 437(7) CrPC), if at any time after conclusion of trial and before judgment, the court is of opinion that there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is NOT guilty:
options: It shall release the accused, if in custody, on execution of a bond without sureties for his appearance to hear judgment
Must pronounce judgment immediately without waiting
Must remand him to police custody
Must dismiss the defence counsel
explanation: Section 480(7) BNSS / S. 437(7) CrPC mandates release on personal bond pending judgment if court forms opinion that accused is not guilty.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; release on personal bond to hear judgment.

learningObjective: Recall release pending judgment under S. 437(7) CrPC.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 436A CrPC (maximum period for which an undertrial prisoner can be detained)?
options: Section 479 BNSS
Section 436A BNSS
Section 480 BNSS
Section 482 BNSS
explanation: Section 479 BNSS corresponds to Section 436A CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 479 BNSS corresponds to Section 436A CrPC.
optionBreakdown.B: No section 436A in BNSS; renumbered S. 479.

learningObjective: Map Section 436A CrPC to Section 479 BNSS.

question: What revolutionary relief does Section 479(1) Proviso BNSS introduce for 'First-Time Offenders' (never convicted of any offence in the past)?
options: A first-time offender shall be released on bail if he has undergone detention for ONE-THIRD (1/3rd) of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for such offence
Shall be released after 24 hours without trial
Shall be released after serving half the sentence
Shall be given a government pension
explanation: Section 479(1) First Proviso BNSS is a monumental humanitarian reform: first-time offenders are entitled to bail upon completing 1/3rd (one-third) of maximum sentence, compared to 1/2 under CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; one-third (1/3rd) threshold for first-time offenders under BNSS S. 479.

learningObjective: Master 1/3rd undertrial bail threshold for first-time offenders in BNSS S. 479.

question: What is the general undertrial detention threshold under Section 479(1) BNSS (Section 436A CrPC) for non-first-time offenders?
options: Detention for a period extending up to ONE-HALF (1/2) of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence
One-fourth of the sentence
Three-fourths of the sentence
Full maximum sentence
explanation: Under Section 479(1) BNSS / S. 436A CrPC, the general rule is release on bail/personal bond upon completing one-half of maximum imprisonment.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; one-half (1/2) of maximum imprisonment.
optionBreakdown.B: 1/4th is not the general undertrial threshold.
optionBreakdown.D: Max period is capped under subsection (2).

learningObjective: Recall general one-half undertrial bail threshold.

question: Under Section 479(2) BNSS, does Section 479 apply to offences for which the punishment of death or life imprisonment is specified by law?
options: No; Section 479 explicitly DOES NOT apply to any offence for which the punishment of death or life imprisonment has been specified by law
Yes, applies equally to murder and terrorism
Applies to death penalty after 14 years
Applies only to offences carrying life imprisonment
explanation: Section 479(1) & (2) BNSS / S. 436A CrPC explicitly excludes offences punishable with death or life imprisonment from automatic undertrial release.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; excluded for offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.
optionBreakdown.B: Death and life offences strictly excluded.
optionBreakdown.C: No automatic undertrial bail in capital cases.

learningObjective: Master statutory exclusion of death/life offences from S. 479 undertrial bail.

question: In In Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons ((2016) 3 SCC 700), what did the Supreme Court direct regarding Undertrial Review Committees (UTRCs)?
options: UTRCs headed by District Judges must meet quarterly to review cases of undertrials entitled to release under Section 436A CrPC and take steps for their immediate release
Prisons should be privatized
All undertrials should be put on forced labor
Section 436A was declared unconstitutional
explanation: The Supreme Court mandated Undertrial Review Committees in every district to systematically identify and release prisoners eligible under Section 436A CrPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Undertrial Review Committees meeting quarterly to enforce S. 436A.

provision: BNSS S. 479 / Inhuman Conditions in Prisons
learningObjective: Master Undertrial Review Committee mandate.

question: What new affirmative duty does Section 479(3) BNSS place on the Superintendent of Jail?
options: The Superintendent of Jail where the accused is detained shall forthwith make an application in writing to the Court for release of such person on bail upon reaching the 1/3rd or 1/2 threshold
The jailer must keep the undertrial in solitary confinement
The jailer must charge a daily lodging fee
The jailer has no duty to track detention dates
explanation: Section 479(3) BNSS imposes a mandatory statutory obligation on the Jail Superintendent to proactively apply to court for release of eligible undertrials.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; mandatory duty on Jail Superintendent to apply for bail for eligible undertrial.

learningObjective: Master proactive jail superintendent bail filing duty under BNSS S. 479(3).

question: In Bhim Singh v. Union of India ((2015) 13 SCC 605), what procedure did the Supreme Court mandate for jurisdictional Magistrates regarding Section 436A CrPC?
options: Magistrates and Sessions Judges must visit jails within their jurisdiction at least once in two months to identify and release prisoners eligible under Section 436A
Judges should never enter prison premises
Police officers should decide who gets released
Undertrial prisoners have no right to judicial visits
explanation: Bhim Singh directed jurisdictional judicial officers to conduct jail sittings every two months to directly pass orders releasing eligible undertrials.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; judicial visits to prisons every two months for on-spot S. 436A release.

learningObjective: Master Bhim Singh jail visits for S. 436A implementation.

question: Under Section 479(2) BNSS, can an undertrial prisoner be detained in prison for a period LONGER than the maximum period of imprisonment provided for the offence?
options: No person shall in any case be detained during the period of investigation, inquiry or trial for more than the maximum period of imprisonment provided for the said offence
Yes, he can be detained indefinitely until trial ends
Yes, if the prosecutor requests it
Yes, up to double the maximum punishment
explanation: Section 479(2) BNSS / S. 436A Proviso CrPC enacts an absolute statutory ceiling: in NO case can an undertrial be detained longer than the maximum sentence for the offence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; absolute bar on detention exceeding maximum punishment.

learningObjective: Master absolute statutory ceiling on undertrial detention.

question: Does Section 479 BNSS (Section 436A CrPC) apply retrospectively to pending cases where trials commenced prior to 1 July 2024?
options: Yes, the Supreme Court held in Re: Inhuman Conditions in Prisons (2024 order) that Section 479 BNSS (including the 1/3rd threshold for first-time offenders) applies retrospectively to all pending undertrials regardless of offence date
No, applies only to crimes committed after 1 July 2024
Applies only to new FIRs
Retrospective benefit was denied by Parliament
explanation: The Supreme Court in August 2024 clarified that Section 479 BNSS is a beneficial procedural provision and its 1/3rd first-time offender benefit applies to all pending undertrials across India.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; applies retrospectively to all pending undertrials across India.
optionBreakdown.B: Beneficial procedural law applies to pending proceedings.

learningObjective: Master retrospective application of BNSS S. 479 1/3rd threshold to pending undertrials.

question: What happens if delay in the trial has been caused by the accused person himself under the Proviso to Section 479(1) BNSS?
options: The court may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, order continued detention beyond the half or 1/3rd period, or release on bail with conditions
The accused is sentenced to life imprisonment
The accused loses Indian citizenship
The court must dismiss the charges
explanation: The Proviso permits court to order continued detention where delay in proceedings was occasioned by the accused person himself, recording reasons.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; court may order continued detention if delay caused by accused.

provision: BNSS S. 479(1) Proviso / CrPC S. 436A Proviso
learningObjective: Recall exception where undertrial causes delay in trial.

question: Under Section 479 BNSS, what form of release can the Court order for an eligible undertrial prisoner?
options: Release on bail on his personal bond with or without sureties
Release only on cash deposit of Rs 5 lakhs
Release only with GPS electronic ankle monitor
Release on condition of cleaning court premises
explanation: Section 479(1) BNSS / S. 436A CrPC provides for release on personal bond with or without sureties.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; personal bond with or without sureties.
optionBreakdown.D: Community service applies to substantive sentencing, not bail bond.

learningObjective: Recall mode of release under S. 479 BNSS.

question: In Hussainara Khatoon (I) v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar ((1980) 1 SCC 81), what constitutional right was recognized under Article 21?
options: Right to speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Article 21, and prolonged detention of undertrials without trial violates personal liberty
Prisons should be closed completely
Accused has no right to speedy trial in India
All criminal cases lapse after 6 months
explanation: Hussainara Khatoon is the historic locus classicus establishing that speedy trial is a fundamental right under Article 21, leading to nationwide undertrial release.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; right to speedy trial is a fundamental right under Art 21.

learningObjective: Master Hussainara Khatoon speedy trial doctrine.

question: If an accused is charged with multiple offences in different cases, does Section 479 BNSS mandate his release across all cases automatically?
options: No; undertrial bail under Section 479 applies to each case independently where detention in that specific case satisfies the statutory period
Yes, release in one case automatically releases him from all other cases
No, if multiple cases are pending, Section 479 is completely barred
Only if the High Court consolidates all cases
explanation: Bail under S. 436A / S. 479 operates qua the specific case and detention suffered therein; it does not automatically discharge production warrants in separate cases.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; operates qua each case independently.
optionBreakdown.B: Production warrants in other cases remain alive.
optionBreakdown.C: Multiple cases do not bar S. 479 if detention threshold met in that case.

learningObjective: Apply Section 479 to multiple pending prosecutions.

question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Satender Kumar Antil ((2022) 10 SCC 51) regarding the role of trial courts in implementing Section 436A CrPC?
options: Trial courts must not wait for applications to be filed by undertrials; they should suo motu identify eligible undertrials and release them on bail
Trial courts must wait for undertrial to engage a senior advocate
Courts can reject 436A bail if the case is sensational
436A is only a recommendation
explanation: Satender Kumar Antil directed trial courts to act suo motu to enforce S. 436A without waiting for formal applications from indigent undertrials.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; suo motu duty of trial courts to enforce S. 436A.
optionBreakdown.B: Indigent accused rarely have senior advocates.

learningObjective: Master suo motu implementation of undertrial bail.

question: Under Section 479 BNSS, who must be given an opportunity of being heard before an order of release is passed?
options: The Public Prosecutor
The District Magistrate personally
The Chief Justice of India
The media reporters
explanation: Section 479(1) BNSS mandates hearing the Public Prosecutor before ordering release on bail under this section.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Public Prosecutor must be given an opportunity of being heard.

learningObjective: Recall requirement to hear Public Prosecutor under S. 479 BNSS.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 438 CrPC (direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest / Anticipatory Bail)?
options: Section 482 BNSS
Section 438 BNSS
Section 484 BNSS
Section 528 BNSS
explanation: Section 482 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 438 CrPC (Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 482 BNSS corresponds to Section 438 CrPC.
optionBreakdown.B: No section 438 in BNSS for anticipatory bail (renumbered S. 482).

learningObjective: Map Section 438 CrPC (Anticipatory Bail) to Section 482 BNSS.

question: Which courts possess concurrent jurisdiction to grant Anticipatory Bail under Section 482 BNSS (Section 438 CrPC)?
options: The High Court and the Court of Session
The Chief Judicial Magistrate and Sessions Court
The Judicial Magistrate First Class only
The Supreme Court exclusively
explanation: Section 482 BNSS (Section 438 CrPC) provides concurrent original jurisdiction strictly to the High Court or the Court of Session.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; High Court and Court of Session have concurrent jurisdiction.
optionBreakdown.B: CJM has no power of anticipatory bail.
optionBreakdown.D: High Court and Sessions have direct original jurisdiction.

learningObjective: Recall courts having anticipatory bail jurisdiction.

question: In the Constitution Bench decision of Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab ((1980) 2 SCC 565), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding Anticipatory Bail?
options: Anticipatory bail is a facet of personal liberty under Article 21; the power under Section 438 is wide and should not be fettered by narrow, artificial judicial restrictions
Anticipatory bail can only be granted in exceptional murder cases
Anticipatory bail must always be limited to 7 days
Anticipatory bail is unconstitutional
explanation: Sibbia Constitution Bench ruled that Section 438 is a wide charter of personal liberty that should not be encumbered by restrictive judicial conditions.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; wide charter of personal liberty under Art 21 free from artificial restrictions.

learningObjective: Master Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia anticipatory bail doctrine.

question: In Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) ((2020) 5 SCC 1), what did the Constitution Bench settle regarding the duration of Anticipatory Bail?
options: Anticipatory bail does not automatically expire upon filing of charge-sheet or framing of charge; it can continue till the conclusion of trial unless special circumstances warrant limitation
Anticipatory bail must strictly terminate after 30 days
Anticipatory bail ends automatically when charge-sheet is filed
Anticipatory bail is valid only for 24 hours
explanation: Sushila Aggarwal Constitution Bench settled the long-standing conflict: anticipatory bail ordinarily continues until the conclusion of trial and does not end with charge-sheet.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; ordinarily continues till conclusion of trial.
optionBreakdown.B: Time cap rejected as general rule.
optionBreakdown.C: Charge-sheet does not automatically terminate bail.

learningObjective: Master Sushila Aggarwal ruling on duration of anticipatory bail.

question: Can Anticipatory Bail be granted after an accused has already been physically arrested by the police?
options: No; anticipatory bail can only be granted to a person apprehending arrest; once arrested, only regular bail under Section 437/439 CrPC (S. 480/483 BNSS) is maintainable
Yes, can be granted at any time during life imprisonment
Yes, after conviction in trial
Police can convert arrest into anticipatory bail
explanation: Anticipatory bail is insurance against impending arrest; once actual arrest occurs, the person is in custody and remedy is regular bail.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; inapplicable once arrested; regular bail applies.
optionBreakdown.C: Post-conviction remedy is suspension of sentence under S. 389.

learningObjective: Master pre-arrest prerequisite for anticipatory bail.

question: Under Section 482(2) BNSS (Section 438(2) CrPC), what statutory conditions may the High Court or Sessions Court include in an anticipatory bail order?
options: (i) Make himself available for interrogation by police as required; (ii) Not tamper with witnesses; (iii) Not leave India without previous permission of court
Must deposit his passport and Rs 50 lakhs cash
Must confess to the crime before a notary
Must remain inside his house 24 hours a day
explanation: Section 482(2) BNSS / S. 438(2) CrPC specifies conditions: availability for interrogation, non-tampering with witnesses, and travel restrictions.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; availability for interrogation, non-tampering, travel restrictions.

learningObjective: Recall statutory conditions in anticipatory bail.

question: Under Section 438(4) CrPC (and BNSS S. 482), is Anticipatory Bail available for offences of rape of a child under 16 or 12 years (Sections 376AB, 376DA, 376DB IPC / BNS S. 65, 70(2))?
options: No; anticipatory bail is barred by statutory exclusion for offences of aggravated rape of children under 16/12 years
Yes, available in all rape cases equally
Available if the applicant pays Rs 10 lakhs
Available with approval of Sessions Judge
explanation: Section 438(4) CrPC (introduced by Criminal Law Amendment Act 2018) expressly bars anticipatory bail for aggravated child rape offences.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory bar on anticipatory bail for child rape offences.
optionBreakdown.D: Sessions Judge cannot override statutory bar.

learningObjective: Master statutory bar on anticipatory bail for child rape.

question: Which provision of BNSS 2023 corresponds to Section 439 CrPC (Special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail)?
options: Section 483 BNSS
Section 439 BNSS
Section 480 BNSS
Section 528 BNSS
explanation: Section 483 BNSS corresponds directly to Section 439 CrPC (Special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 483 BNSS corresponds to Section 439 CrPC.

learningObjective: Map Section 439 CrPC to Section 483 BNSS.

question: Under Section 483(1)(b) BNSS (Section 439(1)(b) CrPC), what special power does the High Court or Court of Session possess regarding conditions imposed by a Magistrate?
options: May set aside or modify any condition imposed by a Magistrate when releasing any person on bail
Can enhance the punishment by 5 years
Can order immediate re-arrest without hearing
Can dissolve the Magistrate's court
explanation: Section 483(1)(b) BNSS / S. 439(1)(b) CrPC empowers Sessions Court or High Court to set aside or modify onerous/unreasonable bail conditions imposed by a Magistrate.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; set aside or modify any bail condition imposed by Magistrate.
optionBreakdown.B: Cannot enhance sentence on bail application.

learningObjective: Recall power to modify onerous bail conditions.

question: Under Section 483(2) BNSS (Section 439(2) CrPC), who can cancel bail granted to any person?
options: A High Court or Court of Session may direct that any person who has been released on bail be arrested and commit him to custody
Any Sub-Inspector of police
The complainant's family
The District Magistrate on administrative order
explanation: Section 483(2) BNSS / S. 439(2) CrPC empowers High Court or Court of Session to cancel bail and commit the accused to custody.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; High Court or Court of Session may cancel bail and arrest.
optionBreakdown.D: DM has no power to cancel judicial bail.

learningObjective: Recall cancellation of bail power under S. 439(2) CrPC / S. 483(2) BNSS.

question: Under Section 413 BNSS (Section 372 CrPC), what is the basic rule regarding Appeals in criminal cases?
options: No appeal shall lie from any judgment or order of a criminal court except as provided for by this Sanhita or by any other law for the time being in force
Appeal lies automatically in every criminal case to Supreme Court
The losing party can appeal to the District Magistrate
Appeals are entirely unconstitutional
explanation: Section 413 BNSS / S. 372 CrPC lays down the fundamental principle: appeal is a statutory creation; no appeal lies unless expressly provided by statute.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; no appeal lies except as provided by statute.
optionBreakdown.B: Appeal is creature of statute, not automatic to SC.

learningObjective: Master principle: Appeal is a creature of statute.

question: Under the Proviso to Section 413 BNSS (Section 372 CrPC), what statutory right of appeal is conferred on the 'Victim'?
options: Right to prefer an appeal against any order acquitting the accused, or convicting for a lesser offence, or imposing inadequate compensation
Right to demand death penalty in all cases
Right to veto the Public Prosecutor
Right to appeal directly to the President of India
explanation: Proviso to S. 413 BNSS / S. 372 CrPC confers three distinct appeal rights on victim: (1) against acquittal; (2) against lesser offence conviction; (3) against inadequate compensation (Mallikarjun Kodagali v. State of Karnataka).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; victim's right to appeal against acquittal, lesser offence, or inadequate compensation.
optionBreakdown.B: Cannot demand death penalty outside law.
optionBreakdown.D: President is executive clemency, not appellate court.

provision: BNSS S. 413 Proviso / CrPC S. 372 Proviso / Mallikarjun Kodagali
learningObjective: Master victim's statutory right of appeal under S. 372 Proviso.

question: Under Section 416 BNSS (Section 375 CrPC), does an appeal lie when the accused has pleaded guilty and been convicted on such plea?
options: No appeal shall lie if conviction is by High Court; and if by Sessions Court or Magistrate, an appeal lies ONLY as to the extent or legality of the sentence
No appeal lies on any ground whatsoever in any court
Full appeal on facts and merits lies to High Court
Accused can retract plea in appeal and get automatic acquittal
explanation: Section 416 BNSS (Section 375 CrPC) bars appeal against conviction on plea of guilty, EXCEPT as to the extent or legality of sentence.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; appeal barred except as to extent or legality of sentence.
optionBreakdown.D: Plea cannot be casually retracted to get acquittal.

learningObjective: Master limited appeal on plea of guilty under S. 375 CrPC.

question: Under Section 417 BNSS (Section 376 CrPC), in which 'Petty Cases' is there NO APPEAL?
options: High Court passes sentence of imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 1,000; Sessions Judge passes imprisonment up to 3 months or fine up to Rs 200; Magistrate First Class passes fine up to Rs 100
Whenever the accused is unemployed
Whenever the trial was conducted in English
Whenever the complainant fails to attend
explanation: Section 417 BNSS (Section 376 CrPC) lists petty cases where no appeal lies based on petty sentence thresholds.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; petty sentence thresholds bar appeal under S. 376 CrPC.

learningObjective: Recall petty case appeal bar under S. 376 CrPC / S. 417 BNSS.

question: Under Section 419 BNSS (Section 378 CrPC), an appeal against an order of acquittal in a case instituted upon a police report can be filed in the High Court:
options: Only by the State Government directing the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal, or by the Central Government in cases investigated by central agency
By any police constable
By any stranger on a public road
Only with approval of the Law Minister
explanation: Section 419 BNSS (Section 378 CrPC) provides that State/Central Government directs Public Prosecutor to present an appeal against acquittal to High Court.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; State/Central Government directs Public Prosecutor to appeal.
optionBreakdown.D: Public Prosecutor files on government direction.

learningObjective: Recall procedure for appeal against acquittal under S. 378 CrPC.

question: Under Section 419(4) BNSS (Section 378(4) CrPC), if an order of acquittal is passed in a case instituted upon a PRIVATE COMPLAINT, how can the complainant appeal?
options: Must apply for and obtain 'Special Leave to Appeal' from the High Court
Can file an appeal directly in the Sessions Court as a matter of right
Can appeal to the District Magistrate
No appeal is permissible for a private complainant
explanation: Section 419(4) BNSS / S. 378(4) CrPC mandates that complainant in private case must apply for and obtain Special Leave to Appeal from High Court.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; application for Special Leave to Appeal to High Court.
optionBreakdown.B: Direct appeal without special leave barred under S. 378(4).

learningObjective: Master Special Leave to Appeal requirement in private complaint acquittals.

question: Under Section 430 BNSS (Section 389 CrPC), pending an appeal by a convicted person, what may the Appellate Court order?
options: Execution of the sentence or order appealed against be suspended and, also, if he be in confinement, that he be released on bail, or on his own bond
The sentence be doubled immediately
The trial be started from scratch before a new magistrate
The appellant be barred from meeting his advocate
explanation: Section 430 BNSS (Section 389 CrPC) provides for suspension of sentence and grant of bail pending appeal by the appellate court.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; suspension of sentence and release on bail pending appeal.
optionBreakdown.C: No de novo trial without setting aside.

learningObjective: Recall suspension of sentence pending appeal under S. 389 CrPC.

question: Under Section 438 BNSS (Section 397(2) CrPC), what is the statutory bar on the exercise of powers of revision by High Court or Sessions Judge?
options: The powers of revision shall not be exercised in relation to any interlocutory order passed in any appeal, inquiry, trial or other proceeding
Revision is barred against final judgments
Revision is barred in all murder cases
Revision is barred if the fine exceeds Rs 1,000
explanation: Section 438(2) BNSS / S. 397(2) CrPC creates an absolute statutory bar: powers of revision shall NOT be exercised in relation to any 'interlocutory order'.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; revision barred against interlocutory orders.
optionBreakdown.B: Revision is available against final orders.
optionBreakdown.D: Fine amount does not bar revision.

learningObjective: Master statutory bar on revision against interlocutory orders.

question: In Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency v. CBI ((2018) 16 SCC 299) and its recent overruling by Constitution Bench in High Court Bar Association Allahabad (2024), what is the law regarding automatic vacation of stay orders?
options: Automatic vacation of stay after six months was declared unconstitutional by the 5-Judge Constitution Bench in 2024; stay orders remain in force until heard and decided on merits
Stay orders automatically expire after 14 days
High Court has no power to grant stay
Stay can only be granted by the Supreme Court
explanation: The 5-Judge Constitution Bench in High Court Bar Association Allahabad (2024) overruled Asian Resurfacing, holding that automatic vacation of stay violates judicial discretion and Article 21.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; automatic vacation of stay overruled by Constitution Bench in 2024.
optionBreakdown.C: High Court has inherent stay powers.

learningObjective: Master 2024 Constitution Bench overruling on automatic vacation of stay.

question: Under Section 442(3) BNSS (Section 401(3) CrPC), what is the express limitation on the High Court in the exercise of its Revisional Jurisdiction?
options: Nothing in this section shall be deemed to authorise a High Court to convert a finding of acquittal into one of conviction
High Court can convert acquittal into conviction directly without appeal
High Court cannot reduce any sentence
High Court cannot call for records
explanation: Section 442(3) BNSS / S. 401(3) CrPC contains a crucial safeguard: High Court in revision CANNOT convert a finding of acquittal into conviction (must order retrial or wait for regular appeal under S. 378).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; High Court in revision cannot convert acquittal into conviction.
optionBreakdown.D: Calling for records is the essence of revision.

learningObjective: Master express bar on converting acquittal into conviction in revision.
